quotes.text: When Brian Wilson convinced the other members (his brothers Carl and Dennis, his cousin Mike Love, and others that floated in and out) to let him retire from touring in order to let him stay home and take a little more time in the songwriting process than he'd been granted previously (also coinciding with when he first started making use of pharmacological creative assistants), the results were often magical; the best material from Today, Summer Days and Summer Nights and especially Pet Sounds stands up to the best material from anybody else in the era.

Unfortunately for Brian and for everybody, though, the creative fire that he lit within himself to write that music ultimately consumed him; his attempt to create the greatest rock album ever made (the aborted Smile project) ultimately manifested in some spectacular material and a bunch of half-finished curiosities, and the inability of the band to finish the project (as well as the terrifying amount of illegal substances he was using) helped push Brian into an increasingly reclusive state.

Brian had been their primary (hell, "primary" might be understating it) songwriter since the earliest days of the band, and with his decline (and the sad truth that, by this point, the band had lost commercial relevance) it would have been perfectly reasonable for the band to disband or, at the very least, immediately start making terrible albums.

The band suddenly became a democratic unit, with everybody pitching in just enough above-average material to pair with Brian's contributions (sometimes muted versions of his previous genius, sometimes collaborations with others, and sometimes leftovers from the Smile sessions) to get their albums up to an acceptable length without too much sacrifice of quality.
Somehow, The Beach Boys transformed themselves into a proto-indie pop band, and while I wouldn't go so far as to call this my favorite era of the band, I can definitely understand why somebody would.

Even though the band members had lived way too hard since the early 60s to write and perform that kind of music in a way that wouldn't seem hopelessly hokey and forced, they tried anyway, and the results were predictably disappointing.

During the band's commercial (and eventually artistic) apex during the 60s, there wasn't a tremendous amount of variety in the band's sound on a given album, and their instrumental abilities were certainly competent but not especially noteworthy, but they had two major positives going for them.

the smartest thing Brian Wilson ever did was ditch Mike Love as a songwriting partner, if he hadn't Pet Sounds would have just been exquisitely arranged songs about amusement parks and looking at girls. I will always maintain that Pet Sounds could never have been the masterpiece it was if Brian hadn't ditched his lame cousin for Tony Asher.

Songs about sun, surf, and girls could get you a long ways in the early 60s, but by 1965 rock music had started to grow up a little bit, and the "Be True to Your School" guys needed to kick it up a notch. And Mike Love was never going to be able to do that.
The Rolling Stone Album Guide writers had bought into that narrative of Brian Wilson building from triumph to triumph until he reached the creative pinnacle of Pet Sounds and "Good Vibrations".
the Beach Boys created some of the most innovative and complex music of the 1960s - only the Beatles were as consistently groundbreaking.
Brian Wilson, more than any other rock musician, bears the striking similarity in his approach to Romantic-era classical composers, and above all has the talent to pull it off.
When he claimed that he was writing "Teenage Symphonies To God" he wasn't kidding.
listen to the arrangements, the texture, the dazzlingly ahead of its time production, the melodies, and above all those gorgeous, stunningly sophisticated vocal harmonies.
Brian Wilson's first flash of genius, this epitomizes everything the early Beach Boys were about.
"The Girls On The Beach" changes keys so much it'll drive you crazy, and demonstrates Brian's burgeoning talent.
The great step forward on the journey towards Pet Sounds.
So as long as Brian and Mike were the ones writing the songs, high school level was about as sophisticated as it was going to get.

It isn't the arrangements that make these albums different really – sure, Today! rocks out where Pet Sounds would never deign to, there was never going to be "Dance, Dance, Dance" or "Do You Wanna Dance" type rockin' arrangements on that album. That said, the songs on Today! have exceptional arrangements.
In an alternate universe Brian Wilson might have been the King of Heavy Metal Riffage.
Brian Wilson was at his peak as a producer and arranger.

In truth, it is only the lyrics and overall messages of the songs that create that yawning gap between Today! and Pet Sounds. If Brian Wilson had started working with Tony Asher a year and a half earlier, the two albums would be on the same level.

The Beach Boys were never going to make an album any better than Today! so long as Mike Love was involved in the songwriting. To get to the next level, Brian was going to need a lyricist worthy of his melodic talents.
Even the songs on side one display a level of melodic brilliance that could have transcended what they are, had those songs not been hopelessly hobbled by lyrical immaturity.

I find it fascinating that Brian realized he could improve the song, and the later version from Summer Days (and Summer Nights!!) we all know and love is vastly better. There's something to be said for recognizing a song isn't quite there, and putting in the work to help it reach its full potential.
